summary: Swiss food giant Nestlé aggressively marketed infant formula as superior to breast milk in poor countries from the mid-20th century, leading mothers to mix it with unsafe water or dilute it and contributing to mass infant malnutrition and death.
keywords: International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes

evidence.note: Henri Nestlé completes his just-add-water formula in 1867
1960s-70s: mothercraft nurses sent into hospitals in poor nations
urban Uganda and Congo named as main promotion targets; Nigeria ads
Ivory Coast case of a starving formula-fed infant and hospital retaliation
Jamaican mother diluting formula, testimony to a US Senate subcommittee
ad campaigns shaming mothers about inadequate breast milk
studies on higher illness and mortality among formula-fed infants
1981 WHO marketing code; 1991 LA Times report follows
2018 Changing Markets report and WHA resolution fight extend coverage to 2018

notes: Main span 1960-1991 chosen as the peak global-South marketing period through the Ivory Coast coverage; aggressive promotion arguably starts in the 1930s. Wet-nursing history (1700s) treated as background. Other formula makers (Abbott, Ross, Bristol-Myers) discussed but not listed as subjects.
